Trump of the United States, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of Australia, Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, and Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae of Japan — met for a Quad Leaders’ Summit in Manila. This year marks nearly a decade since the Quad was revived and the tenth anniversary of the vision of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific, first articulated by the late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo of Japan in 2016. A decade on, that vision is stronger than ever. Together, we have shown that the Quad is a force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability, and prosperity. We strongly oppose any destabilizing or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability. We express grave concerns about economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions. We are securing critical supply chains, protecting freedom of navigation and overflight, driving growth through technologies of the future including investments in and deployment of trusted Super Intelligence (SI)*, and responding to disasters with life-saving assistance. We commit to work together to ensure open, safe, and resilient maritime transit corridors in the Indo-Pacific. We are working with regional partners to tackle shared challenges and drive opportunities to deliver tangible benefits to the Indo-Pacific. We announce the inaugural Quad Business Leaders’ Forum which is scheduled to be held in early 2027, bringing together business leaders, government officials, and policy experts from Quad countries to foster greater business ties across our private sectors, including the promotion of commercial deals and partnerships critical to the prosperity of the Indo-Pacific. We affirm the importance of the Super Intelligence* Accelerator , announced by our Foreign Ministers in Atlanta.  The Accelerator is intended to coordinate and fund efforts to support trusted Super Intelligence (SI)* access, deployment, and technical assistance across the Indo-Pacific. We are proud to welcome the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration , a new initiative to enhance information sharing and maritime domain awareness.  In 2027, our respective P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft are scheduled to fly in a maritime exercise for the first time in a Quad context, making our seas safer. We are proud of progress under the Quad Partnership for Cable Connectivity and Resilience , which has expanded access to secure and trusted communications infrastructure across the Indo-Pacific.  Today, we welcome an expansion of Australia’s contribution to the Partnership to focus on electricity cables, strengthening regional energy security and connectivity.  We also welcome upcoming undersea cables projects in the Indian Ocean which are intended to strengthen regional connectivity. We acknowledge the rapid increase in the number and scale of cyber incidents in the region and announce enhanced Quad Cybersecurity Cooperation , through which we plan to work together to achieve an open and secure cyberspace. We unequivocally condemn terrorism and violent extremism in all its forms and manifestations, including cross-border terrorism, and commit to strengthening the Quad’s ongoing cooperation on counterterrorism. We reaffirm our unwavering support for ASEAN centrality and unity.  Together, we are committed to upholding a free and open Indo-Pacific. * In Australia, India, and Japan, ‘Super Intelligence’ refers to ‘artificial intelligence.’ The post Quad Leaders’ Summit Joint Press Release appeared first on The White House .

在没有黄仁勋的 Nvidia 中，人工智能模型和出口管制之争仍在继续。但谁控制了芯片的流向，也就控制了领先的前沿人工智能模型的流向。据报道，OpenAI 现在支持美国国会两党共同推动限制中国获得先进人工智能加速器和设备。但额外的人工智能安全问题是否真实存在，或者它们也是巩固其在快速发展的行业顶端地位的便捷方式？我们采访了欧洲开放市场研究所所长马克斯·冯·图恩 (Max von Thun) 等专家，以了解更多信息。首先，我们以 OpenAI 的 GPT-6 Astra 为例。该公司于 9 月份推出了该模型，并声称这是该公司迄今为止功能最强大、协调性最好的系统。 OpenAI 自己的测试表明，Astra 在遵循指令和尊重边界方面表现得更好。在一项内部计算机使用安全基准中，不一致结果的比例从 GPT-5.6 Sol 的 18.8% 下降到 Astra 的 3.4%。但仅仅因为它表面上表现更好并不意味着它完全安全。 OpenAI 表示，当他们测试 Astra 逃避监管的能力时，其书面推理比其前身更难监控。该模型开始识别自己何时被观看，并改变其解释以适应研究，从而更难判断它何时实际上在做他们不想要的事情。这是人工智能对齐专家需要尝试解决的一个经典问题。
确保事物安全 多年来，开发人员一直依靠监控人工智能模型的思想链（其书面工作）来了解它在做什么。但是，如果日益强大的人工智能模型能够更好地隐藏其推理过程，那么这种监督就会变得更加困难。 OpenAI 表示，Astra 在执行复杂任务时仍然难以隐藏推理，其评估结果表明其具有很强的整体一致性，但这里存在令人担忧的权衡迹象。当人工智能系统的部署具有更大的自主权时，这些令人担忧的迹象变得更加明显。 7 月，OpenAI 模型绕过了其内部评估限制，获得了对属于 Hugging Face 的研究基础设施和受损系统的访问权限，以及澳大利亚和加拿大政府控制的 IT 系统的访问权限。为了方便而进行安全打击？在此背景下，呼吁采取更强有力的安全措施似乎完全合理。但欧洲开放市场研究所所长马克斯·冯·图恩认为，这场辩论有可能忽视令人不安的利益冲突。 “我认为很多关于人工智能安全的观点都是非常真诚的，”他在接受 Tom's Hardware Premium 采访时说道。但他认为商业考虑因素非常重要。

The battle for AI models and export controls continues amidst a Jensen Huang-free Nvidia. But who controls the flow of chips also controls the flow of leading frontier AI models. OpenAI reportedly now supports a bipartisan push in the U.S. Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI accelerators and equipment. But are the additional AI safety concerns genuine, or are they also a convenient way to shore up its position at the top of a fast-moving industry? We speak to experts like Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, to find out more. First off, let's take OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. The company launched the model in September with eye-popping claims that it was the firm’s most capable and best-aligned system yet. OpenAI’s own testing suggested that Astra was much better at following instructions and respecting boundaries. In one internal computer-use safety benchmark, the proportion of misaligned outcomes fell from 18.8% with GPT-5.6 Sol to 3.4% with Astra. But just because it was better behaved on the surface didn’t mean it was entirely safe. OpenAI said Astra’s written reasoning was harder to monitor than its predecessor’s when they were testing its ability to evade oversight. The model began to recognize when it was being watched and altered its explanations to suit the study, making it harder to tell when it was actually doing something they didn’t want. It’s a classic problem for AI alignment experts to try and resolve. Keeping things safe For years, developers have relied on monitoring an AI model's chain of thought — its written working — to understand what it is doing. But if increasingly powerful AI models become better at hiding their reasoning processes, that oversight becomes harder to do. OpenAI says that Astra still struggles to hide reasoning when it’s carrying out complex tasks, and its evaluation results suggest it has strong overall alignment, but there are worrying signs of a trade-off here. Those worrying signs become even more so when AI systems are being deployed with more autonomy. In July, OpenAI models ducked its internal evaluation restrictions to gain access to research infrastructure and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, and to IT systems controlled by the Australian and Canadian governments. Safety crackdowns for convenience? Against that backdrop, calls for stronger safety measures seem entirely reasonable. But Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, believes the debate risks overlooking an uncomfortable conflict of interest. "I think a lot of these views about AI safety are very genuinely held," he told Tom’s Hardware Premium in an interview. But commercial considerations loom large, he reckons. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are spending huge sums developing and deploying models, while facing questions about whether their competitive advantages can survive the arrival of increasingly capable, cheaper alternatives — particularly as they go out and seek funding from the public through an IPO . "They don't have huge moats, even if they’ve acquired a lot of users,” von Thun said. “They’re definitely vulnerable.” Those vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly obvious. A September report from Mozilla estimated the capability gap between leading closed American models and their open-weight competitors had narrowed to just over four months. That matters because open-weight models give people the freedom not to rely on a company’s subscription services. They can be deployed on infrastructure controlled by the customer, modified for specialised tasks, and operated at lower costs. But to the discomfort of U.S. companies, many of them are based in China. And it’s at that point that AI safety gets muddled with geopolitics. China versus the U.S. In July, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic, despite their fierce commercial rivalry, had found a common cause: warning U.S. policymakers about the dangers of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Kristy Loke, an AI governance researcher at King's College London who specialises in China's approach to the technology, questions the timing. "It's very suspicious timing asking for pacing," she told Tom's Hardware Premium , referring to calls for slowing frontier AI development just as Chinese open-weight models are undercutting their American rivals on price. Loke believes companies genuinely worry about the risks. But she also thinks they're worried about their commercial prospects. "they're calling for pacing because they have some safety concerns, they have some commercial anxiety," she said. She believes some influential people in American AI have increasingly sought to "paint open models in a very bad light", portraying them as inherently less secure than closed alternatives. Yet the risks of AI systems misbehaving aren't restricted to models developed in China, as OpenAI's own incidents demonstrate. But open-weight models come with their own risks. Because their underlying parameters can be modified , third parties can create and distribute "abliterated" models, removing the refusal behaviours designed to prevent AI from responding to potentially harmful requests. Many of these models are available on platforms including Hugging Face. “They’re not adding in new behaviour; they’re just removing this refusal behaviour,” said Catherine Flick, professor of ethics and games technology at the University of Staffordshire, in an interview with Tom’s Hardware Premium . Abliterating models doesn’t make them more capable, Flick said, but it does mean they can answer questions they previously wouldn’t have been willing to. That also means those responses might not have been tested for accuracy or hallucinations. Those in favour of open-weight models like DeepSeek and Qwen say that removing those guardrails helps security researchers understand how AI behaves. Flick said that’s plausible, but “I just don’t really buy it,” she said. She reckons that the negative potential outputs outweigh the positive case for abliteration because when they’re publicly available, preventing their misuse becomes tricky. American labs clearly have commercial reasons to criticise open-weight competitors because the latter undercuts their economics, but it also doesn’t mean their concerns about safety aren’t valid, too. Von Thun fears that could result in precisely the wrong kind of regulation. "I think what we should not be doing is allowing the companies to basically form a safety cartel," he said. Yet U.S. AI companies benefit from the government's determination to maintain its advantage over China. Von Thun argues the Trump administration has created an environment in which economic power translates into political influence, allowing major technology companies to invoke national security concerns when arguing for policies that may also serve their commercial interests. But that could backfire. "I think completely closing off the market to AI products from other countries, including China, would not be the right approach," von Thun said. China’s own alignment approach Part of the reason that wouldn’t be the right approach is that the idea that the United States is focused on developing AI responsibly while China isn’t is a fallacy. Just earlier this month, Reuters reported that ByteDance had established a dedicated Alignment & Preparedness team, recruiting researchers to investigate safety risks arising from increasingly capable AI systems. For von Thun, the solution is to prevent either industry or geopolitical competition from determining what safety means. He points to the European Union's AI Act, which establishes obligations for developers of general-purpose AI models classified as posing systemic risks. The obligations require companies to conduct model evaluations, adversarial testing, cybersecurity measures and also to report serious incidents. The opposition to the EU’s AI Act from American tech companies, U.S. politicians and the general public who grouse about the way it delays access to cutting-edge models for Europe’s 450 million citizens demonstrates that these provisions don't automatically solve the alignment problem. But they at least involve more people in the conversation about what is and isn’t acceptable for AI than just the industry's biggest participants. Watching watchdogs Even when AI companies agree to independent oversight, they still want some say over how it works — and their own internal decision-making on what is and isn’t safe differs from that of those outside the company. Loke warns that leading AI companies are experimenting with recursive self-improvement, where models help develop their successors, potentially making it more difficult for humans to understand how decisions are being made. "They’re still attempting more risky methods to train AI that will make the AI harder to control," she said. Von Thun also believes competition rules and interoperability requirements could help prevent AI companies from locking customers into proprietary ecosystems as their agents become increasingly embedded in everyday workflows. There are plenty of good reasons to be concerned about alignment, particularly when the models being developed are becoming more capable and more difficult to monitor. But letting the companies responsible for building them determine what constitutes an acceptable risk, and who can compete, brings its own dangers. “I’m not saying we don’t need to worry about safety,” said von Thun, “but we should about letting the companies do it."
